summary: Granite light at the harbour entrance of Rose Blanche, southwest Newfoundland, lit 1873 or 1874 by John A. Roberts. Fell into ruin after its keepers left; rebuilt 1996-99 and open in summer.

lens.where: inside the tower (a Canadian Coast Guard gift per the society; LighthouseFriends says it was given to the restoration workers)
lens.note: The original 1874 apparatus was a fourth-order dioptric lens showing a fixed white light (LighthouseFriends; society)

structures.note: 12 m (40 ft) octagonal granite tower with lantern and gallery, rising from one end of the 1.5-storey granite keeper's house (Rowlett; LighthouseFriends). Rebuilt 1996-99 reusing most original stone.
Collapsed October 1957 (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett); the residence was rebuilt in the 1996-99 restoration and now houses a community museum (heritage statement)
Open-frame tower in the 1940s beside the old lighthouse (LighthouseFriends); Rowlett: wood skeletal tower in the early 1940s
Steel skeletal tower in the early 1960s (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett; society)

staffing.note: Lightkeepers ended in the early 1940s by the heritage and society accounts; LighthouseFriends and Rowlett put the final deactivation in the 1980s.

access.note: Operated by Rose Blanche Lighthouse, Inc. The lighthouse and tower are open daily early June to late September, for an admission fee.

facts.agency: Rose Blanche Lighthouse, Inc. (site operator); Canadian Coast Guard (light)

events.note: Petition for lighthouses in the Burgeo and LaPoile districts presented to the House of Assembly on 21 February 1871, with Rose Blanche residents among the petitioners (second-hand, via the society)
Inspector J.T. Neville selects the site on 26 July 1871
Granite tower and keeper's house built by Smith and Haw(e); the heritage statement dates the work 1871-1873, LighthouseFriends says it was built in the summer of 1873
Lit for the first time 1 January 1874 by John A. Roberts (LighthouseFriends; heritage statement); the society says 1873
Fourth-order dioptric lens, fixed white, 29 m focal plane, visible 13 miles; apparatus designed and supplied by D. and T. Stevenson
Small outside kitchen added to the keeper's dwelling
Fall 1889 accident: lens considerably damaged; keeper Roberts' hands badly burned
Southern and eastern sides painted with red and white vertical stripes
New lens installed to replace the old apparatus
Particularly fierce storm in August 1939 severely damaged the lighthouse
Decommissioned in the early 1940s, before Confederation, per the heritage statement and society; LighthouseFriends and Rowlett put deactivation in the 1980s
Keeper's dwelling collapsed in October 1957 (LighthouseFriends: in a puff of dust; Rowlett: during a storm); the tower stood
Southwest Coast Development Association identifies the ruined station for tourism development
Restoration begins in the fall of 1996; about 70 per cent of original stones reused
Flashing red light donated by the Canadian Coast Guard activated 3 August 2002
Registered Heritage Structure, provincial; society gives 7 September 2002, the first lighthouse in the province so recognised
150th anniversary of the light station celebrated in July 2023

corrections.proposed: Built 1871-1873 (heritage statement; society); first lit 1 January 1874 (LighthouseFriends; heritage statement); reconstructed 1996-1999
corrections.why: The brief's 1996 date is the start of the restoration. Rowlett says '1996 (reconstructed 1873 lighthouse)'. The original tower and house date from 1871-1873.

corrections.proposed: octagonal granite light tower with lantern and gallery, 12 m, rising from one end of a 1.5-storey granite keeper's house
corrections.why: Rowlett describes an octagonal granite light tower; the heritage statement calls it an octagonal light tower; LighthouseFriends says it rose from one corner of the dwelling. Nothing in the sources says conical.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends and the heritage statement give 1 January 1874 (John A. Roberts). The society's history says the light was lit for the first time in 1873. Both are reported; the story does not choose.
The heritage statement and the society give 1871-1873. LighthouseFriends says the house was constructed during the summer of 1873. Reported as stated.

The society says either Robert Oake or J.T. Neville designed the house; the heritage statement says likely J.T. Neville; LighthouseFriends names the Stevensons for the lantern and apparatus, not the house. Reported without choosing.

The heritage statement and the society say the lightkeepers and the original light ended in the early 1940s. LighthouseFriends and Rowlett have the skeletal towers carrying a light until the light was deactivated in the 1980s. Both reported.

LighthouseFriends says the house collapsed in October 1957 in a puff of dust; Rowlett says it collapsed during a storm that October; the heritage statement says all but collapsed in a 1957 storm. Reported as a disagreement about the cause.
The society says five keepers; its own list names six stints, with Philip Hatcher serving twice. The LighthouseFriends roster also has six stints. The story names each stint.
LighthouseFriends' roster starts Bruce Cook in 1910; its text and the society say 1909. The keeper record uses 1909 with a note.

notes_for_editor: Dates and attributions disagree across the four main sources (see resolved_conflicts); each is reported in the story. The society's history is a community site and quotes the 1871 Journal of the House of Assembly second-hand; the Journal itself was not reached. The Canadian Register of Historic Places entry 2095 returned no readable text and is not cited. The Heritage Foundation's Rose Blanche page was read; the heritage.nf.ca article timed out. Not reached: Newfoundland newspapers (1939 storm, 1957 collapse, 1889 accident), Coast Guard station files for the 1940s decommissioning, and the Parks Canada register. The 'Robert Oake' attribution rests on the society alone. Bruce, Minnie, Hatcher and Skinner are historical figures; no living family members are named. The 'one of only 27' lens figure is the society's and the heritage statement's, not independently checked.
